strengths: The core idea is interesting and well-motivated: quantifying token-level visual dependency (via KL divergence between output distributions conditioned on original vs. perturbed images) and using it to modulate the learning signal at both trajectory and token levels addresses a real, underexplored problem in multimodal RLVR.

The empirical evaluation is unusually thorough: eight benchmarks across 7B and 32B scales, comparisons against a large suite of recent RL-tuned open-source models, and an extensive set of ablations (component ablations of TAS/TGF, filtering ratio k, shaping range, masking strategy, dependency metric choice, entropy penalty, group size, and comparison against entropy-based and random token selection).

The comparison against entropy-based token selection (Table 4) is a valuable and convincing experiment that directly tests the paper's central claim that visually-grounded pivotal tokens differ from the high-entropy 'forking tokens' studied in text-only RL.
Insights 1 and 2 (sparse token dependency distribution; heterogeneous trajectory-level grounding) are empirically grounded and provide a useful analytical lens for multimodal RLVR.
Reproducibility is supported by detailed hyperparameter tables, a full training algorithm, prompt templates, and discussion of compute resources and overhead.
weaknesses: Novelty is overstated. Token-level credit assignment in RL is well studied (high-entropy minority tokens, critical token contrastive estimation), and PAPO (Wang et al., 2025e) already targets perception-aware signals for multimodal RL. The claim of being 'the first multimodal RL algorithm to identify perceptually pivotal tokens' is not well supported given this closely related concurrent work.

The proposed mechanism is relatively simple (advantage rescaling by a batch-normalized saliency score plus a binary top-k% gradient mask), and its effectiveness may partly come from effects generic to any signal modulation; the random-selection baseline in Table 4 still improves over DAPO, suggesting part of the gain is not specific to visual dependency.

The theoretical analysis (Theorem 3.1) is essentially trivial under its assumptions: discarding gradients from 60% of tokens and rescaling the advantage reduces the second moment by construction. Variance reduction alone is not evidence of a better estimator (a zero estimator has zero variance); the theorem does not address whether the removed gradient signal was useful, which is the actual empirical question.

There is a conceptual mismatch in the dependency metric: token saliency is computed by re-running the policy on the masked image while conditioning on a trajectory generated from the original image (an off-policy/counterfactual pass), so the measured KL conflates visual dependency with the model's sensitivity to any perturbation; the paper does not analyze this bias.

Internal inconsistency between the analysis and the method: Insight 1 claims only a 'small critical minority' of tokens have high visual dependency, yet the method retains the top k=40% of tokens as 'pivotal,' which undermines the sparsity narrative and suggests k was chosen empirically rather than from the insight.

Headline claims are inflated: the '19.2% average improvement' is relative to the untuned base model, while the improvement over the strongest competing baseline (PAPO-D) is about 2.2 points; no statistical significance, error bars, or multiple seeds are reported despite the modest margins.

Baseline comparisons mix author reproductions with different training configurations (e.g., different rollout counts, NoisyRollout trained on Geo3k training set), which weakens the fairness of direct numeric comparisons in Table 1.

Generalization is limited to verifiable math/geometry/logic benchmarks; the paper itself acknowledges applicability to open-ended multimodal tasks is unclear, and no non-math benchmark (e.g., grounding, general VQA) is evaluated to test whether 'visual dependency' truly improves perception beyond test-domain-specific gains.

strengths: The paper is well-motivated: identifying that RLVR for LVLMs broadcasts a uniform outcome-based signal to all tokens, ignoring which tokens actually depend on visual evidence, is a reasonable and clearly articulated angle.
VPPO is simple and modular: trajectory-level advantage shaping (TAS) and token-level gradient filtering (TGF) can be plugged into existing RLVR recipes (GRPO/DAPO), which increases practical appeal.

The empirical evaluation is extensive: eight benchmarks, two model scales (7B and 32B), comparisons against many recent RL-tuned baselines, exact-match scoring with a fixed evaluation pipeline, and avg@8 reporting.

The ablation suite is unusually thorough for this line of work: component ablations (Table 2), sensitivity to k (Fig. 6) and to the shaping range (Table 3), guidance-signal controls vs. entropy and random token selection (Table 4), masking-strategy ablation (Table 7), dependency-metric ablation (Table 8), group-size ablation (Table 9), and an entropy-penalty study (Table 6, Fig. 9). The comparison against entropy-based 'forking token' selection is a particularly relevant control.
Reproducibility is decent: hyperparameters, compute, framework (EasyR1), prompt template, and pseudocode (Algorithm 1) are provided; limitations and the ~10% training overhead are honestly reported.
weaknesses: Limited novelty. Both components are straightforward heuristics: advantage rescaling and top-k% gradient masking. Prior work already covers closely related ground (PAPO for perception-aware optimization; 'Beyond the 80/20 rule' for high-entropy minority-token filtering; Vassoyan et al. for critical-token exploration). The claim of being 'the first' multimodal RL algorithm to identify perceptually pivotal tokens is overclaimed and mainly reduces to substituting an entropy score with a KL-based visual-dependency score.

The core dependency metric is questionable. Visual dependency is measured as KL divergence between output distributions under the true image vs. a randomly blackened image (50% of patches). This conflates genuine visual grounding with generic sensitivity to input corruption/noise; the paper does not validate that high-dependency tokens are causally linked to correct perception beyond a single qualitative example (Fig. 7).

The theoretical contribution (Theorem 3.1) is close to vacuous. Reducing variance by multiplying the gradient by k * E[alpha^2] < 1 is a trivial consequence of scaling down any estimator; the assumptions (uncorrelated per-step gradients, advantage independence, second-moment dominance) are strong and unverified, and no bias/SNR analysis is provided. Low variance of a biased, shrunken estimator does not imply better optimization.

An inconsistency between narrative and method: the paper claims a 'sparse' set of pivotal tokens, but the default k = 0.4 means 40% of tokens receive gradients. It is unclear why 40% qualifies as sparse, and the analysis in Sec. 3.2.1 (extremely skewed dependency distribution) is not actually reflected in the chosen hyperparameter.

Baseline fairness concerns: several competitor rows are the authors' own reproductions (marked with daggers), and NoisyRollout is trained on a Geo3k training set that overlaps an evaluation benchmark (footnoted). The headline '19.2% average improvement' is measured against the untuned base model rather than against the strongest RL baseline (the actual margin over PAPO-D is ~2.2%), which inflates the perceived contribution.

Evaluation is heavily skewed toward mathematical/geometry reasoning (six of eight benchmarks), a domain where the training set (ViRL39K) and several benchmarks (e.g., MMK12 from MM-Eureka) have close lineage; contamination/generalization concerns are not fully addressed, and the claimed gains on the more general benchmarks (MMMU-Pro: +2.0 over DAPO) are much smaller than the aggregate number suggests.

Insights 1 and 2 are largely expected: it is unsurprising that most tokens have low visual dependency and that trajectories vary in visual grounding. The empirical distribution figures support the observations but the analysis is descriptive (one model, one benchmark subset) rather than establishing that uniform-signal training actually fails for the stated reason.

Writing/positioning issues: heavy use of superlatives ('pioneering', 'first attempt', 'profound stability benefits'), the Figure 8 example is presented sloppily, and the paper does not sufficiently engage with how VPPO differs in outcome from PAPO-D beyond the aggregate numbers.

strengths: The paper introduces a clear and well-motivated perspective on multimodal RLVR: quantifying token-level visual dependency via KL divergence between output distributions conditioned on the true vs. perturbed image, and using this signal at both the trajectory level (advantage shaping) and the token level (gradient masking).

Strong empirical evaluation: eight diverse benchmarks, two model scales (7B and 32B), exact-match scoring with avg@8, and comparisons against many recent strong open-source RL-tuned models (DAPO, MM-Eureka, VL-Rethinker, NoisyRollout, PAPO-D, etc.). The gains (57.5 avg at 7B, 64.6 at 32B) are substantial.

Extensive and unusually thorough ablation studies covering the filtering ratio k, the shaping range [βmin, βmax], masking strategy, dependency metric (KL vs. JSD vs. Top-1 drop), rollout group size, and an important analysis of the entropy penalty required to stabilize the baseline. The comparison against entropy-based token selection and random masking directly supports the claim that visual dependency (not just token salience) is the useful signal.

The manuscript is well organized, includes pseudocode (Algorithm 1), detailed hyperparameter tables, prompt templates, and an honest limitations section (compute overhead, scale, domain scope), supporting reproducibility.
The qualitative case studies in the appendix are informative and clearly annotated to explain baseline failure modes.
weaknesses: The theoretical analysis (Theorem 3.1) is weak in substance: under its assumptions it essentially shows that scaling and masking the gradient reduces the second moment (i.e., the gradient norm), which is trivially true of any masked/scaled estimator. It does not establish improved signal-to-noise ratio or faster optimization; reducing gradient magnitude also reduces update strength, so 'variance reduction' alone does not imply a better learning signal. Assumption 2 (advantage independent of per-step gradients) is also questionable since the advantage depends on the same trajectory.

Tension between the motivating analysis and the method: Insight 1 argues that only a small, critical minority of tokens have high visual dependency, yet the optimal filtering ratio is k = 0.4 (40% of tokens), which is not sparse and undercuts the 'sparse pivotal tokens' narrative. This inconsistency should be better explained.

Novelty positioning is somewhat overstated. The 'first attempt' and 'pivotal token' claims need to be more carefully delineated against existing work on perception-aware RL (e.g., PAPO, visual perception rewards), high-entropy minority tokens (Wang et al., 2025c), and contrastive token-level credit assignment (Lin et al., 2024). The core idea—restricting/weighting gradients by a token-level importance signal—is a natural instantiation of known ideas; the contribution is more in the visual-dependency metric and the combination of mechanisms than in a fundamentally new algorithmic principle.

Empirical gaps: no standard deviations or significance tests across seeds are reported, and several benchmark gains over the strongest baseline (e.g., +2.5 avg over PAPO-D) may be within noise. The TAS component alone yields only ~1.3% average gain, and its interaction with batch-level normalization (βmax = Dyn.) is under-analyzed.

The masked-image forward pass is only for the current policy; dependency is computed from πθold distributions, so the mask and shaping are stale relative to the update, and the method's sensitivity to this staleness is not discussed. Additionally, the dependency metric could be gamed or confounded by model priors (a token can be image-dependent yet wrong), which is not analyzed.

Some presentation issues: Table 1 mixes reproduced numbers (†) with self-claimed results and includes footnoted caveats (NoisyRollout trained on Geo3k's training set) that complicate exact comparability; the 'Project Page' placeholder is empty in the submission.

strengths: Clear and well-motivated core idea: quantifying per-token visual dependency via KL divergence between output distributions conditioned on the true vs. perturbed image, and using it to modulate the learning signal at both trajectory (advantage shaping) and token (gradient filtering) levels.

Strong empirical evaluation: eight benchmarks spanning math, geometry, logic, and multi-discipline reasoning, at both 7B and 32B scales, with consistent gains over GRPO/DAPO baselines and strong reproduced open-source competitors.

Above-average ablation coverage for this area: component ablations (TAS/TGF), filtering ratio k, shaping range, dependency metric choice (KL vs. JSD vs. probability drop), image perturbation strategy, binary vs. soft mask, reward vs. advantage shaping, rollout group size, entropy penalty, and generalization to GRPO.

Fair-comparison efforts: equal computational-budget comparison (Table 15) addressing the ~10% overhead of the second forward pass, plus out-of-domain VQA evaluation showing no degradation of general capabilities.
The empirical analysis (Insights 1-2) on the sparse, long-tailed distribution of token perception and heterogeneity across trajectories is a useful contribution to understanding multimodal RLVR.
Reproducibility support: pseudocode, full hyperparameter table, prompt templates, and a stated anonymous code release.
weaknesses: Novelty is incremental. Token-level credit assignment via selective optimization already exists for text RL (e.g., high-entropy 'forking tokens', Lin et al. 2024, both cited), and perception-aware objectives in multimodal RL (e.g., PAPO, perception rewards) are close relatives. The main novelty reduces to swapping the token-selection signal from entropy to an image-perturbation-based dependency score, combined with standard advantage reweighting. The repeated 'first attempt' claims are overstated.

The theoretical analysis (Theorem 3.1) is weak: the variance reduction follows trivially from dropping a k-fraction of gradient terms under strong and unrealistic assumptions (uncorrelated per-step gradients, independence between advantage, shaping factor, and gradients). Reducing variance by discarding gradients says nothing about bias or the direction/quality of the learning signal, and the framing overstates its significance.

No statistical significance testing or variance reporting: improvements over the strongest baselines on individual benchmarks are often ~1-2 points with avg@8 evaluation; without seeds/CI it is hard to judge robustness of some margins.

The key hyperparameters (k=0.4, beta range, entropy penalty coefficient 0.06) appear tuned on the evaluation-adjacent setup, and the paper acknowledges re-tuning may be needed elsewhere; gains are sensitive to these choices per the ablations.

The dependency metric may conflate genuine visual grounding with model-specific artifacts (e.g., tokens where the perturbed image destabilizes the policy), and the method's reliance on the model itself to define 'perception' creates a potential self-reinforcing loop during training that is not analyzed.
Validation is confined to verifiable-reward, reasoning-heavy tasks on one model family (Qwen2.5-VL); applicability to other domains, subjective tasks, or other architectures remains untested.

Baseline reproductions rely on 'official author-provided prompts', and some competitor entries carry footnotes (e.g., NoisyRollout trained on Geo3k training set), making cross-method comparisons slightly uneven despite the fixed evaluation pipeline.

strengths: The core idea is intuitive and well-motivated: token-level visual dependency (KL divergence between predictions conditioned on the original vs. perturbed image) provides a principled signal for identifying perceptually pivotal tokens in multimodal RLVR.

The empirical evaluation is extensive: eight benchmarks, two model scales (7B and 32B), consistent gains over GRPO/DAPO baselines, comparison with many recent open-source RL-tuned models, plus out-of-domain VQA checks.

The ablation studies are unusually thorough: component-wise ablations (TAS/TGF), sensitivity to filtering ratio k and shaping range, comparison against entropy-based and random token selection, soft vs. binary masking, dependency metric choice, masking strategy, group size, and a fixed-compute equal-budget comparison (Table 15) that addresses the ~10% training overhead concern.

The two insights (sparse token dependency distribution; heterogeneous trajectory-level grounding) are clearly presented and supported by distribution analysis, and the method design follows directly from them.
The method is pluggable into existing RLVR algorithms (demonstrated on both GRPO and DAPO), and implementation details/hyperparameters are provided for reproducibility.
weaknesses: Limited novelty and overstated claims. The 'pioneering exploration' and 'first attempt' framing is not accurate: PAPO (Wang et al., 2025e) already incorporates perception-aware signals into multimodal RL optimization and is used as both a baseline and the source of the training recipe; V-Triune/One-RL (Ma et al., 2025) uses per-modality advantage computation; several token-level selection works (high-entropy minority tokens, critical tokens) are close relatives. The contribution is essentially applying an image-perturbation KL probe to select tokens/weight trajectories, which is a natural combination of existing ingredients.

The theoretical analysis (Theorem 3.1) is weak and largely cosmetic. Masking tokens does not produce an unbiased variance-reduced estimator of the same quantity — it changes the estimator itself, so comparing 'variance' (actually second moments, under a dominance assumption) conflates reduced noise with reduced signal. Assumptions 1-3 (uncorrelated per-step gradients, advantage independence, dependency-advantage independence) are strong and unjustified in practice; α(τ) is by construction correlated with reward statistics within a batch. No evidence is provided that the k·E[α²] factor is actually <1 empirically or that variance reduction translates to learning improvement.

Gains over the most relevant baseline are modest and statistical significance is never established. The margin over entropy-based token selection (57.1 vs. 56.0 avg@8) and over the full-method ablations (~1 point) is within plausible run-to-run variance; no error bars, seeds, or significance tests are reported anywhere despite avg@8 evaluation.

The visual dependency estimate is itself noisy and unvalidated against ground truth: random patch blackening with p=0.5 makes the KL score a single-sample stochastic estimate, and there is no direct measurement of whether high-dependency tokens actually correspond to perceptually critical information beyond one qualitative example (Figure 7).

The advantage shaping normalizes α(τ) by batch min/max of trajectory dependency, making the shaping factor dependent on batch composition and introducing additional stochasticity into the learning signal; this is not analyzed.

The evaluation is confined to math/geometry/logic-style verifiable benchmarks where binary exact-match rewards work; the applicability to the broader multimodal RL setting is acknowledged but untested, which narrows the claimed significance of the 'multimodal RLVR' framing.

The paper's positioning that baselines 'broadcast a uniform learning signal' slightly mischaracterizes DAPO's token-level loss normalization, and the baseline reproduction details († re-runs) raise questions about whether all compared methods received identical tuning effort.

Presentation issues: the writing is promotional in tone, several sections read as LLM-polished boilerplate, and Figure 8's 'catastrophic collapse' example (with mixed-language gibberish) is presented anecdotally without systematic characterization of collapse frequency.

strengths: The paper introduces a clear and well-motivated perspective: quantifying token-level visual dependency via KL divergence between output distributions conditioned on the original vs. perturbed image, and using this to reshape both trajectory-level advantages (TAS) and token-level gradients (TGF).

The two empirical insights (sparse token-level dependency distribution; heterogeneous trajectory-level dependency) are grounded in direct analysis (Figures 3-4) and directly motivate the algorithmic design.

Comprehensive evaluation: eight diverse benchmarks, two model scales (7B and 32B), strong open-source baselines (DAPO, MM-Eureka, VL-Rethinker, NoisyRollout, PAPO-D, etc.), exact-match scoring, and avg@8 reporting with a fixed evaluation pipeline.

Extensive ablations: component ablations (TAS/TGF), sensitivity to k and [β_min, β_max], entropy guidance vs. visual dependency vs. random token selection, binary vs. soft masks, advantage vs. reward shaping, masking strategy, dependency metric (KL vs. JS vs. Top-1 drop), group size, and a compute-equalized comparison showing the ~10% overhead does not explain the gains.
Generality is supported: VPPO is applied on top of both DAPO and GRPO with consistent gains, and positive transfer to out-of-domain VQA (A-OKVQA, SimpleVQA) is shown.
Reproducibility is strong: full hyperparameter table, pseudocode (Algorithm 1), anonymous code, prompt templates, and computational resource details.
weaknesses: Novelty is more incremental than the 'first attempt' framing suggests. Perception-aware policy optimization (PAPO, Wang et al. 2025e) is a direct predecessor that also injects perception-awareness into the RL signal; token-level credit assignment via entropy/contrastive estimation (Wang et al. 2025c; Lin et al. 2024) is well established. The contribution is a modality-specific instantiation of these ideas rather than a fundamentally new mechanism, and positioning against PAPO could be sharpened.

The theoretical analysis is weak. The 'Variance Reduction' result (Theorem 3.1) follows almost immediately from restrictive assumptions (uncorrelated gradients, second-moment dominance) and is essentially the observation that a 0/1 mask reduces the number of summed gradient terms. It also ignores that gradient filtering introduces bias (the estimator is no longer unbiased for the original objective), which is the more important theoretical question and is not addressed.

The headline 19.2% improvement is relative to the base model (38.3 to 57.5); the meaningful improvement over the strongest baseline (DAPO) is 2.5 points on average, and over PAPO-D 2.2 points. These gains, while consistent, are moderate and within the range that run-to-run variance in RL training could influence; statistical significance or multiple seeds are not reported.

The visual dependency metric is defined with respect to the policy itself (KL between the policy's own distributions), creating a degree of circularity: the model may under-weight tokens it has already learned to predict confidently regardless of true visual grounding, and the metric's validity as a measure of 'visual dependency' is validated mainly downstream rather than against ground-truth perceptual requirements.

There are small internal inconsistencies/oddities: e.g., TGF-only lowers MMK12 relative to baseline (80.9 vs 82.1) while raising other benchmarks; the DAPO entropy penalty of 0.06 is a nonstandard and quite strong regularizer added to both methods, making the comparison slightly dependent on this shared choice (though this is disclosed and ablated).
Only the empirical trajectory/token distribution analysis is performed on MathVerse with a 7B model; the insights are not shown to hold across domains or scales before motivating the method.

Reproducibility details are good, but key hyperparameters (k=0.4, dynamic β_max) were tuned on the training setup and the authors acknowledge they may require re-tuning elsewhere; some sensitivity remains unquantified across datasets.
